Q: Regridding emmeans() after an orderNorm() transform A:

I'm not familiar with the orderNorm function, but your ord_tran list needs to be actual mathematical functions of one variable, and you need to include at least linkfun, linkinv, mu.eta, and valideta. mu.eta is the derivative of linkinv and is needed to do the delta method.

Try running make.link("sqrt") to see an example.

But I'm thinking that orderNorm() might be some kind of rank-based function on a set of data, in which case I think it may not be possible to specify an inverse and its derivative in the required form.

Q: How can I find/identify large commits in Git history? A:

None of the other powershell answers worked for files with spaces. This worked for me:

git rev-list --objects --all --missing=print |
 git cat-file --batch-check="%(objectsize) %(rest)" |
 ? { $_ -match "^(\d+)\s+(.+)$" } |
 % { [pscustomobject] @{ "Path" = $Matches[2]; "Size" = [long]$Matches[1] } } |
 sort -Property "Size" |
 % { echo "$($_.Size) $($_.Path)" } |
 Select-Object -Last 10

Q: In 2026, what field should a computer engineering student focus on, and what roadmap should they take? A:

The truth is that nobody can predict the future. My general advice would be put your head down, try to get good grades and build cool projects.

The recent systems that are making waves in software (like claude code) are developed using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, which is a technique that improves performance when you have a clearly specifiable problem and an easily checkable solution (think "write a function that does "x"). These systems cannot create new algorithms or architectures not represented in their training set. They are also not too hot at system design because of world modelling limitations.

Fortunately for us there are plenty of tasks you face as a software engineer that are ambiguous, and require creativity and systems thinking. I would avoid tying too much of your career capital into memorizing specific libraries or syntax as this is becoming devalued. Try to build complex systems that interact with the real world and require deep conceptual understanding of the fundamentals, instead of writing boilerplate stuff.

Agentic coding seems to introduce a lot of security issues, so the one thing I'm confident about is that there will be an increased demand for cybersecurity professionals in the future. For general dev jobs, I think as our productivity increases, we should be more in demand, although the job likely looks different due to AI.
